Well-motivated multi-teacher design with convincing ablations showing each teacher contributes non-redundant signals (Table 9)
Strong empirical results on multiple benchmarks with 3.2% improvement over SceneSplat on ScanNet200 semantic segmentation
Thoughtful domain-specific engineering: 3DGS-aware augmentations demonstrate principled design rather than naive point cloud adaptation
Practical render-and-distill adaptation that eliminates 1TB storage overhead for pseudo-label preprocessing

Data efficiency improvements claimed (8.32× and 39.9× fewer training scenes than point cloud baselines)

Incremental over SceneSplat [28]: core novelty is adding multiple teachers rather than fundamental conceptual advance; modest improvements of 1-3% on several benchmarks
Contradictory evidence undermines core 3DGS argument: point cloud variant using only center/color/normal is competitive with Sonata, questioning necessity of full 3DGS parameters

Unfair data efficiency comparisons: claims 8.32×/39.9× efficiency over point cloud methods trained on different data; cannot isolate whether gains come from multi-teacher approach vs. 3DGS data vs. different training distribution

Insufficient complementarity analysis: Table 9 shows each teacher helps but lacks investigation of redundancies, interaction effects, or what each specifically contributes beyond aggregate gains
Modest improvements in key metrics: linear probing shows only 1.5 mIoU gain over Sonata on ScanNet Val (75.2 vs. 73.7); instance segmentation results mixed and sometimes smaller than baselines
Experimental comparison concerns: Table 1 uses varying training data multipliers (×1 to ×2.92); no error bars or statistical significance testing; new InteriorGS benchmark only evaluated by Chorus
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to indoor scenes; no outdoor scene understanding or analysis of generalization across diverse scene types; no failure mode analysis
Reproducibility issues: code unavailable during review, key implementation details in inaccessible supplement, design choices lack justification, no sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse tasks (semantic/instance segmentation, open-vocabulary, VQA), datasets (ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, InteriorGS), and thorough ablations validating all design choices

Strong empirical results with significant data efficiency: 8.32× fewer training scenes than point cloud baselines and 39.9× fewer than Sonata on point clouds, while achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance
Well-motivated 3DGS-aware augmentations (rendering-equivalent and immature-manifold perturbations) grounded in rendering equations and optimization dynamics, avoiding ad-hoc point cloud augmentations
Practical render-and-distill adaptation eliminates ~1TB preprocessing storage, adds only 0.1s/view overhead, and enables lightweight out-of-domain finetuning—valuable engineering contribution
Technically sound methodology: proper normalized uplifting (Eq. 3), PHI-S teacher standardization, staged teacher introduction with clear justification
Clear presentation with informative visualizations (Figure 1-3) and comprehensive supplementary results; work should be reproducible
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: multi-teacher distillation and 2D-to-3D feature lifting are established techniques (RadioV2, AM-RADIO, DUNE in 2D; SceneSplat in 3D); main contribution is application to 3DGS rather than fundamental advance

Point cloud variant's impressive performance (matching/exceeding Sonata with 39.9× fewer scenes) is underexplored and appears somewhat accidental: the noise robustness experiment (Table 8) uses only 684 instances from 10 scenes, and the 'strong augmentation' hypothesis is speculative since augmentations were designed for 3DGS rendering, not noise robustness
Narrow evaluation scope limited to indoor scenes only (ScanNet, Matterport3D, InteriorGS); no outdoor evaluation or cross-domain generalization studies, limiting claims about broader applicability

Strong dependence on frozen 2D foundation models (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial) with limited exploration of teacher selection sensitivity; ablation of teachers (Table 9) is superficial and doesn't address how to select/combine teachers for new domains

Computational overhead not fully addressed: model size (131.3M params) is larger than SceneSplat (91.7M) and Mosaic3D (39.1M); slowest inference time (0.70s/scene); end-to-end training time vs. baselines and preprocessing cost not quantified

Loss balancing and teacher standardization design choices lack rigorous justification: PHI-S choice not compared to alternatives, equal loss weights (λt=1.0) work empirically but optimality unclear, no multi-task learning analysis

Staged teacher introduction (PE-Spatial added in second half outperforms adding from start) suggests training dynamics matter significantly, but this is underexplored with limited investigation of staging schedules
Modest improvements on some tasks: VQA gains are marginal (Table 3: +0.4 EM@1 for ScanQA, -0.4 METEOR), and instance segmentation results are competitive but not consistently dominant

strengths: Well-motivated multi-teacher pretraining framework with clear justification for combining language-aligned, generalist, and object-aware teachers to capture complementary semantic dimensions

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ScanNet, Matterport3D, InteriorGS), diverse downstream tasks (semantic/instance segmentation, VQA, open-vocabulary), and modalities (point clouds), with strong ablation studies validating design choices
Significant practical data efficiency: achieves 39.9× fewer training scenes compared to single-dataset pretraining baselines
Strong empirical results on multiple benchmarks, particularly excelling on ScanNet and open-vocabulary tasks, with unexpected robustness to point cloud transfer despite 3DGS-based training
Thoughtful rendering-based adaptation recipe (Algorithm 1) enabling efficient out-of-domain finetuning without expensive 3D pseudo-labels, with clear pose sampling and visibility culling strategies
Excellent reproducibility support: detailed implementation details across 6-page appendix, clear algorithmic descriptions, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: multi-teacher knowledge distillation and per-teacher losses (Equations 5-6) are standard; primary contribution is combinatorial rather than methodologically novel

Inconsistent performance gains across benchmarks—SceneSplat outperforms Chorus on ScanNet with full finetuning (26.4 vs 25.8), instance segmentation improvements sometimes marginal, suggesting limited task generalization despite holistic encoding claims

Insufficient justification for design choices: no comparison of alternative teacher combinations, teacher weight λ appears empirically tuned without principled derivation, minimal sensitivity analysis for loss weights (η_n, η_λ) and rendering resolution

Rendering-based adaptation underexplored: evaluated only on semantic/instance segmentation, not other downstream tasks; limited analysis of when adaptation helps vs. hurts; pose sampling strategy (FPS) not compared against alternatives

Data efficiency claims oversold: 39.9× metric compares against per-task 3DGS training rather than other pretraining methods; missing comparisons with alternative 3D pretraining (Point-BERT, DepthContrast); computational cost of pretraining ignored

Point cloud generalization mechanism unexplained: strong transfer to point clouds (Table 2) is surprising but receives minimal analysis beyond brief Section 4.3 mention, lacks investigation of feature space properties explaining cross-modality transfer

Limited evaluation scope: missing important 3D tasks (object detection, panoptic segmentation, tracking), no few-shot/sparse annotation scenarios, no robustness evaluation (domain shift, corrupted inputs), limited modality diversity

Incomplete computational cost analysis: Table 7 reports only inference time; training/pretraining cost comparison absent; memory requirements during multi-teacher pretraining not discussed; claims about training data efficiency confuse with modality transfer

Reproduction complexity: different feature extraction protocols required for each teacher with varying resolutions/embedding sizes (Appendix B.1); hyperparameter sensitivity to teacher-specific choices not analyzed

Ablation study gaps: Table 9 teacher ablation doesn't isolate individual teacher effects; 3DGS-aware augmentation (Section 3.4) lacks detailed ablation explaining necessity of immature manifold perturbation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse tasks (semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, open-vocabulary, VQA) and multiple benchmarks (ScanNet, Matterport3D, InteriorGS)
Demonstrates consistent improvements in low-data regimes, supporting practical data efficiency claims
Well-organized presentation with clear methodology diagrams and thorough supplementary material supporting reproducibility
Extensive ablation studies and qualitative visualizations (Figures 4, 7, 8) providing additional insights into model behavior
Addresses relevant problem of generalizable 3D scene understanding by leveraging multiple 2D foundation models
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing components (3DGS, SigLIP, DINO, PE-Spatial, standard distillation) without introducing new theoretical insights or fundamentally new techniques

Modest performance improvements: most gains are 1-3% across benchmarks; on ScanNet200 Table 1, Chorus matches SceneSplat's baseline at 22.4 mIoU rather than exceeding it. No statistical significance testing provided

Rendering-based adaptation (Section 3.3) feels underdeveloped and rushed; Eq. 8 represents standard supervised rendering without novelty; limited experimental validation of its superiority
Insufficient theoretical analysis: paper lacks principled explanation for why multi-teacher approach should work; no analysis of complementarity between teachers or what different teachers capture
Evaluation limitations: primarily indoor scenes with limited out-of-domain evaluation; no comparison with recent multi-modal 3D methods; robustness to different scene types not systematically tested
Computational cost not addressed: training with three teachers must be expensive, but no training time, memory, or computational efficiency analysis provided; only inference time reported

Architectural choices inadequately justified and analyzed: why shared vs. independent encoders, why these specific projector designs; Table 9 teacher ablation doesn't clearly isolate individual contributions
Architectural novelty concerns: each component (projectors, losses, adaptation) represents straightforward application of existing techniques without innovation
Title overstates contribution: claims 'holistic' encoding, but evaluates specific tasks rather than truly general scene understanding; limited scope with narrow focus on specific benchmarks

Practical rendering-based adaptation method that enables out-of-domain finetuning without expensive 3D pseudo-label preprocessing
Rigorous experimental design with thorough ablations, robustness analysis, and qualitative visualizations demonstrating the effectiveness of design choices
